question: Which hormone relaxes the smooth muscle in the gut during pregnancy?
explanation: You've got this! Progesterone rises high during pregnancy, which naturally relaxes smooth muscles all over the body—including the digestive tract.

question: Why does the body slow down digestion during pregnancy?

options.A: To allow more time for absorbing nutrients
options.B: To keep the maternal body temperature stable
options.C: To reduce pressure on the urinary bladder
options.D: To prevent the stomach from overstretching

explanation: Think of it as a helpful feature: slower digestion gives the body extra time to soak up all those important vitamins and nutrients for the growing baby!

question: Where does the growing uterus usually push the stomach during pregnancy?

options.A: Downward and deep into the pelvis
options.C: Forward against the anterior abdominal wall

explanation: As the baby grows and takes up space below, the stomach gets nudged upward and slightly to the left. Makes sense when you picture it!

question: What is the main reason pregnant women experience heartburn?

options.A: Increased production of hydrochloric acid in the stomach
options.B: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter by progesterone
options.C: Rapid enlargement of the liver pressing on the diaphragm
options.D: Frequent consumption of spicy foods during meals

explanation: Progesterone relaxes the valve right at the top of the stomach, letting acid sneak up into the food pipe (esophagus) and cause that burning feeling.

question: A pregnant patient at 28 weeks complains of severe heartburn after eating. What is the best advice to give her?

options.A: Lie flat on your back immediately after meals to rest your digestion
options.B: Take strong laxatives every evening to empty your bowels completely
options.C: Eat small, frequent meals and avoid lying down right after eating
options.D: Drink large glasses of water with every meal to dilute stomach acid

explanation: Smaller meals keep the stomach from getting overloaded, and staying upright uses gravity to keep the acid where it belongs!

question: Which tummy trouble is most commonly caused by slow digestion and pressure from the uterus?
explanation: You got it! Slower movement means the bowel absorbs extra water, leaving stools hard to pass—plus, the heavy uterus adds extra pressure.

question: Why are pregnant women more likely to get hemorrhoids?

options.A: Loss of sphincter control caused by high estrogen
options.B: Eating too much refined sugar and processed foods
options.C: Increased pelvic venous pressure and straining from constipation
options.D: Direct infection of the rectal mucosa by bacteria

explanation: It's a double whammy: the heavy uterus slows down blood flow from the lower body, and pushing hard due to constipation makes those sensitive veins swell up.

question: What effect does progesterone have on the gallbladder during pregnancy?

options.A: It causes sluggish emptying and bile stasis
options.B: It stops the liver from producing cholesterol
options.C: It causes the gallbladder to shrink significantly
options.D: It speeds up the release of concentrated bile

explanation: Just like the gut, the gallbladder muscles relax too. This makes it empty slower, leaving bile sitting inside longer (stasis).

question: Why is there a higher risk of developing gallstones during pregnancy?

options.A: The growing uterus crushes the bile duct and blocks fluid flow
options.B: The liver stops producing bile salts entirely during the first trimester
options.C: Bile stays in the gallbladder longer and becomes supersaturated with cholesterol
options.D: High iron supplements crystallize inside the biliary tree

explanation: When bile sits around too long and mixes with extra pregnancy cholesterol, it forms stones easily. Makes total sense when you think about it!

question: What happens to digestion when a woman goes into active labour?

options.A: It slows down significantly or stops almost entirely
options.B: It reverses direction, causing constant vomiting
options.C: It remains completely unchanged from normal pre-pregnancy rates
options.D: It speeds up to clear the body for delivery

explanation: The stress and pain of labour naturally put digestion on pause, meaning food stays in the stomach instead of moving along.

question: Why are women in active labour usually advised not to eat heavy solid foods?

options.A: To prevent sudden spikes in blood pressure during contractions
options.B: To keep the bowel completely empty to make room for the baby
options.C: To stop the stomach from producing excessive digestive acid
options.D: To prevent aspiration if vomiting occurs during delivery

explanation: Since food just sits in the stomach during labour, vomiting could cause stomach contents to slip into the lungs. Keeping meals light or restricted keeps mum safe!

question: What hormonal change helps the digestive tract get back to normal after childbirth?

options.A: A rapid drop in progesterone levels
options.B: A continuous high output of estrogen
options.C: A gradual increase in resting cortisol
options.D: A sudden surge in human placental lactogen

explanation: Once the placenta is delivered, progesterone levels drop fast, allowing the digestive tract to bounce right back to its normal tone.

question: What is a very common reason new mothers delay their first bowel movement after delivery?

options.A: Fear of pain from perineal stitches or hemorrhoids
options.B: Severe dehydration that dries out all body fluids
options.C: Complete lack of any urge to defecate for several weeks
options.D: Permanent paralysis of the colon caused by epidural anesthesia

explanation: Spot on. Soreness from stitches or swollen piles can make going to the toilet feel scary, so mums often hold back.

question: Which of these is NOT part of a routine check on a new mother's digestive recovery?

options.A: Asking when she last opened her bowels
options.B: Checking for bowel sounds and passage of gas
options.D: Inspecting the abdomen for signs of surgical wound breakdown

explanation: While surgical wound checks are vital after a C-section, general bowel recovery is all about checking for gas, bowel movements, and comfort down below.

question: A mum on her second day after delivery hasn't passed stool and is scared to use the toilet. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Withhold all oral fluids and food until she passes flatus
options.B: Administer a strong stimulant enema immediately without consulting a doctor
options.C: Insist that she remains in bed until her bowel movement happens naturally
options.D: Encourage fluid intake, walking around, and check if stool softeners were ordered

explanation: Gentle movement, plenty of fluids, and stool softeners are the safest, kindest way to help her first postpartum toilet trip go smoothly!
